content:
On 9 August this year, the Observatory recorded an all-time high of 36.9 degrees, and temperatures in Sheung Shui climbed even higher to 39.8 degrees in the afternoon. I huddled in my narrow flat in the sweltering heat, daring to open the window only a crack. In such extreme heat, the hot wind really does rush back into the home, so I shut the balcony door and all the living room windows tight. I live on a mid-floor between two small hills, and apart from noon, the sun never reaches my flat; without air conditioning, three ceiling fans whir away, bringing a cool breeze through the room. In Hong Kong's heatwave days, you really have to learn to count your blessings.

During the record-breaking scorcher, I did the laundry at home. Just after 1pm, I washed two large bedsheets and duvet covers, four pairs of jeans, and a pile of T-shirts. Two hours later, I flipped the sheets and duvet covers over to dry on the other side. After 6pm, I brought the warm clothes and bedding back indoors — just like taking laundry out of a giant tumble dryer at the laundromat and laying them on the bed. It felt as though I had not experienced such naturally sun-dried, fresh-smelling laundry in half a century. I should have been thinking of my friends out in the blazing sun, but only by doing load after load of washing could I slightly offset the discomfort brought on by the fierce sun.

August has become a nightmare. I do not know how many more Augusts it will take before I can break free from this endlessly repeated summer of farewells. One night in a dream, I walked proudly with my arm linked through my mother's, saying: "My little mummy." I was so happy I held her tight. Before me appeared a woman draped in a deep crimson cloak; my subconscious did not want to see her face clearly, but the dream's镜头 kept zooming in on her face — it was a stranger I did not recognise. Just before waking, a surge of unbridled joy welled up, and what I remember is — I dreamed of my mother again.

On the evening of 10 August 2020, our family sang hymns, kissed my mother's forehead, and bid her farewell. That was a full stop. Yet learning to let go has always been a lifelong lesson. Reluctance is a silent wound. Six years on, there are still a thousand regrets in the details; my mind replays the ins and outs of those days six years ago, over and over.

Regret and reluctance come sooner or later, regardless of age, making their appearance at different stages of life. A student in my writing class wrote about her late grandmother — a piece of remembrance, mourning, or regret. When she was even younger, she had hated staying with her grandmother in the countryside. By day she was a little monster bursting with energy, bickering with her grandmother, who would pinch her ears; she would retaliate, making her grandmother taste her own pain. Then, through a crack in the door, the little girl saw her frail, sickly grandmother secretly wiping away tears. That night the little girl fell ill, running a fever, and in a daze walked up to her grandmother and said: "I don't feel well."

Not feeling well — that's what feeling unwell all over is like, the feeling of a child being sick. She was burning with fever, and her grandmother, without a word, changed her into fresh clothes and immediately carried her on her back to the hospital to queue to see a doctor. The medicinal oil's scent she once detested now lingered faintly with her all the way to the hospital. Then, somehow, that medicinal oil scent faded, and the little girl sat alone near the registration desk waiting. Some adults came over and asked: "Where's your family?" The moment she opened her mouth, tears streamed down her face, until the medicinal oil scent drifted near again; she calmed down and waited properly for the doctor to give her an injection and medicine.

Back home, the scent of medicinal oil was as usual, but somehow it had lost its potency. From the kitchen came the rhythmic sound of meat being chopped on a board, and the aroma of plain congee simmering in the pot. The true meaning of everyday life needs no explanation — it is as plain and clear as this.

I wonder: if I fall ill today, who will cook congee for me?

When I was little, it was usually my father, sometimes my mother, who would patiently hand-slice beef and cook congee for me. This was my sick-day menu, mine alone. Sometimes after seeing the doctor, I would pre-order this minced beef congee: "I want beef and spring onion congee." A privilege reserved only for the sick. Now, no one cooks this congee for me anymore, and when I am ill, I no longer eat this kind of beef congee either.

"If you're sick now, just order takeaway on Foodpanda," a friend said. Other friends cook plain or fish congee for their wives. "I can cook minced pork congee too." "Hand-chopped, not blended in a food processor." "Ready in minutes." Because a pot of congee can make one feel deeply cherished.

"In a lifetime, not many people will cook congee for you when you're sick. Once you grow up, more often it's you cooking for others. Many people go through life this way. Whatever you feel, say your proper goodbye, speak from the heart — those who witness it will all find peace for you," I told my student. She looked at me, a flicker of light in her eyes.

A piece about a grandmother can bring comfort. Father, mother, grandmother… these are the stories we naturally know how to write.

The student's strength was not in polished prose. She seized on medicinal oil as her main thread, weaving around it to express genuine feeling for her closest family. She may not have loved her grandmother the most, but the time together that fate arranged means she cannot forget today everything her grandmother did for her, and cannot help but realise how people grow up unknowingly. In the end she handed in a piece that was deeply moving, and truly made one feel "unwell" in the most affecting sense.

Medicinal oil went from something detested, to something reliable, to something embarrassing, to something worth missing. It turns out that on the student's first day of primary school, classmates laughed at the smell of medicinal oil on her and called her a country bumpkin. She ran home crying and ordered her grandmother to wash every single piece of her clothing from top to bottom with heavy-duty detergent. Her grandmother held the clothes and cried. From when the little girl was eight months old, her grandmother had raised her single-handedly, until she grew up and went to school. After returning to the outside world, the granddaughter seemed to have become a different person, hurting her grandmother's heart. After going back to live with her mother, one day — by which time her grandmother had already developed dementia (Alzheimer's disease) — the student went back with her mother to visit the elderly woman, only to find she was no longer "recognised".

"You can't be my granddaughter — she never liked talking to me," the old woman said to the student.

Life is both real and cruel. Have I ever been so cruel to my mother? It seems not. Perhaps I have, only — like the student — without knowing it. Family members sometimes hurt one another. The point is, from now on, will we learn to love better?
